apmo-2004-01.prompt:
Determine all finite nonempty sets $S$ of positive integers satisfying
$$\frac{i + j}{(i, j)} \quad\text{is an element of } S \text{ for all } i, j \text{ in } S,$$
where $(i, j)$ is the greatest common divisor of $i$ and $j$.
apmo-2004-01.answer: Only $S=\{2\}$. ($i=j$ gives $2\in S$; a largest odd element $k$ would give $k+2\in S$; a smallest element $\ell>2$ would give $\frac\ell2+1\in S$ strictly between $2$ and $\ell$.)

apmo-2004-02.prompt: Let $O$ be the circumcentre and $H$ the orthocentre of an acute triangle $ABC$. Prove that the area of one of the triangles $AOH$, $BOH$ and $COH$ is equal to the sum of the areas of the other two.
apmo-2004-02.answer: Proof: the centroid $G$ lies on line $OH$; if $B,C$ are on the same side of it, the distances satisfy $d(B)+d(C)=2d(M)=d(A)$ ($M$ the midpoint of $BC$, $AG=2GM$), so $[BOH]+[COH]=[AOH]$.

apmo-2004-03.prompt:
Let a set $S$ of $2004$ points in the plane be given, no three of which are collinear. Let $\mathcal{L}$ denote the set of all lines (extended indefinitely in both directions) determined by pairs of points from the set. Show that it is possible to colour the points of $S$ with at most two colours, such that for any points $p, q$ of $S$, the number of lines in $\mathcal{L}$ which separate $p$ from $q$ is odd if and only if $p$ and $q$ have the same colour.

*Note:* A line $\ell$ separates two points $p$ and $q$ if $p$ and $q$ lie on opposite sides of $\ell$ with neither point on $\ell$.
apmo-2004-03.answer: Proof: for any three points $p,q,r$, $n(p,q)+n(q,r)+n(r,p)\equiv 2004-3\equiv1\pmod 2$; so colour $q$ like a fixed $p$ iff $n(p,q)$ is odd.

apmo-2004-04.prompt:
For a real number $x$, let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ stand for the largest integer that is less than or equal to $x$. Prove that
$$\left\lfloor \frac{(n-1)!}{n(n+1)} \right\rfloor$$
is even for every positive integer $n$.
apmo-2004-04.answer: Proof: for $n\le5$ the value is $0$. For $n\ge6$: if $n,n+1$ are both composite then $2n(n+1)\mid(n-1)!$; if $n$ or $n+1$ is a prime $p$, Wilson's theorem shows $(n-1)!+(n+1)$ resp. $(n-1)!+n$ equals $n(n+1)$ times an odd number, so the floor is that odd number minus $1$.

apmo-2004-05.prompt:
Prove that
$$(a^2 + 2)(b^2 + 2)(c^2 + 2) \ge 9(ab + bc + ca)$$
for all real numbers $a, b, c > 0$.
apmo-2004-05.answer: Proof: in fact $(a^2+2)(b^2+2)(c^2+2)\ge3(a+b+c)^2\ge9(ab+bc+ca)$; e.g. if $(a^2-1)(b^2-1)\ge0$ then $(a^2+2)(b^2+2)\ge3(a^2+b^2+1)$, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives $(a^2+b^2+1)(1+1+c^2)\ge(a+b+c)^2$.
